precepts.text: Beware of all whoredom, my son, and chiefly take a wife of the seed of thy fathers, and take not a strange woman to wife, which is not of thy father's tribe. Whoredom falls under fornication; this is what made Esau a fornicator: he married Hittite women and Ishmaelite women, and Ishmael was the beginning of another race; Genesis is the beginning of races. For we are the children of the prophets, Noe, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: our fathers from the beginning all married wives of their own kindred, and were blessed in their children, and their seed shall inherit the land.
precepts.point: Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright. In that pottage was meat: feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage, raw, bloody meat. And you have brothers today lusting after these same people. Many times brothers ask what it means that Esau was profane or a fornicator; the scriptures explain it.
precepts.why:
Tobit 4:12 shows why Esau is called a fornicator: “Beware of all whoredom, my son, and chiefly take a wife of the seed of thy fathers, and take not a strange woman to wife, which is not of thy father’s tribe.” Whoredom falls under fornication. Esau married Hittite women and Ishmaelite women, strange women not of his father's tribe.

Ishmael was the beginning of another race; Genesis is the beginning of races. Tobit goes on: “for we are the children of the prophets, Noe, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: remember, my son, that our fathers from the beginning, even that they all married wives of their own kindred, and were blessed in their children, and their seed shall inherit the land.”

So the fathers married within their own kindred and were blessed in their children; Esau did not. Then there is the profaneness. Hebrews says he sold his birthright “for one morsel of meat”, and that shows what was in the pottage. When Esau came in from the field faint and said, “Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage”, he wanted it as it was, raw, red and bloody. “therefore was his name called Edom”, which means red. He said, “Behold, I am at the point to die: and what profit shall this birthright do to me?” and “thus Esau despised his birthright.” And there are brothers today lusting after these same people and having children with them.

That is why, “when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected”: rejected by God, “for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.”

note.label: In Vain Do They Worship Me! Religious Syncretism

precepts.why:
“But king Solomon loved many strange women, together with the daughter of Pharaoh”. When you turn against the Lord in this, you turn against your neighbor too, because you are taking foreign women. We know it will turn your heart away from following the Lord, but what does it do to your brother? It says you hate your brother. Tobit shows it.

“Beware of all whoredom, my son, and chiefly take a wife of the seed of thy fathers, and take not a strange woman to wife, which is not of thy father’s tribe”. He calls interracial marriage whoredom. “for we are the children of the prophets, Noe, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: remember, my son, that our fathers from the beginning, even that they all married wives of their own kindred, and were blessed in their children, and their seed shall inherit the land.”

“Now therefore, my son, love thy brethren, and despise not in thy heart thy brethren, the sons and daughters of thy people, in not taking a wife of them”. Don’t despise your brethren. Passing over the daughters of your own people for strange women is despising your brethren in your heart. “for in pride is destruction and much trouble, and in lewdness is decay and great want: for lewdness is the mother of famine.”

That is exactly where Solomon went. The Lord had said of those nations, “Ye shall not go in to them, neither shall they come in unto you: for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods”, and Solomon clave unto them in love. His wives turned away his heart after Ashtoreth, Milcom, Chemosh and Molech, and he built high places for them and for all his strange wives. That is how syncretism enters: through the strange wife, and it begins by despising your own people.

precepts.why:
Numbers 36 is the law for the brother who had no sons. The chief fathers of Gilead, of the tribe of Manasseh, came before Moses because the inheritance of Zelophehad was given to his daughters, and “if they be married to any of the sons of the other tribes of the children of Israel, then shall their inheritance be taken from the inheritance of our fathers”. The inheritance goes to her husband. Not even the jubile would bring it back: “so shall their inheritance be taken away from the inheritance of the tribe of our fathers.” You are Manasseh, you marry into Judah, and Judah owns that land forever.

So the Lord commanded, “only to the family of the tribe of their father shall they marry”, “that the children of Israel may enjoy every man the inheritance of his fathers.” That is the law right there: if you have all daughters and you have land and property, they marry within the tribe so another tribe of Israel does not take possession of it forever.

That is what Tobit was making reference to. Brothers often ask, because Judah married outside the tribe of Judah and Ephraim married outside the tribe of Ephraim. But there was a special clause when it came to property and land, and the woman was not allowed to do that.

Tobit tells his son, “chiefly take a wife of the seed of thy fathers, and take not a strange woman to wife, which is not of thy father’s tribe”. See that: not of thy father’s tribe. “for we are the children of the prophets, Noe, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob”, and “our fathers from the beginning, even that they all married wives of their own kindred, and were blessed in their children, and their seed shall inherit the land.” Shall inherit the land: that is the point. Marrying your own kindred is how the inheritance of the fathers stays with their seed.

precepts.text: Take a wife of the seed of thy fathers, as Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob did from the beginning, and their seed shall inherit the land.
precepts.point: Abraham made his eldest servant swear that he would not take a wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites, but go to Abraham's country and kindred. The Most High never condoned marrying into the other nations; the custom was kept from the beginning, way before Moses and Deuteronomy 7:3.
precepts.why:
Abraham made his eldest servant swear “that thou shalt not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell: But thou shalt go unto my country, and to my kindred.” Tobit gives the same charge to his son: “chiefly take a wife of the seed of thy fathers, and take not a strange woman to wife, which is not of thy father’s tribe: for we are the children of the prophets, Noe, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”

And he says how far back it goes: “our fathers from the beginning, even that they all married wives of their own kindred, and were blessed in their children, and their seed shall inherit the land.” The Most High never condoned marrying into the other nations. The custom was kept from the beginning, by Noe, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, way before Moses and Deuteronomy 7:3.

precepts.text: The fathers from the beginning married wives of their own kindred; take a wife of the seed of thy fathers.
precepts.point: With the charge came the blessing of Abraham, passed now to Jacob and his seed: to be fruitful, to multiply into a multitude of people, and to inherit the land promised to Abraham.

note.label: Genesis 28: The Charge and the Vow at Bethel

precepts.why:
Isaac charged Jacob, “Thou shalt not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan”, but to go to the house of Bethuel and take a wife of the daughters of Laban. Tobit shows this was the way of the fathers from the beginning: “take a wife of the seed of thy fathers, and take not a strange woman to wife, which is not of thy father’s tribe: for we are the children of the prophets, Noe, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: remember, my son, that our fathers from the beginning, even that they all married wives of their own kindred, and were blessed in their children, and their seed shall inherit the land.”

Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob married wives of their own kindred and were blessed in their children. And with the charge came the blessing: to be fruitful, to multiply into “a multitude of people”, and to “inherit the land wherein thou art a stranger, which God gave unto Abraham.” Their seed shall inherit the land.

precepts.point: No one today knows his exact tribe with certainty; a Judahite could have been dropped off anywhere in the captivity. Without the history of Numbers 36, Tobit 4:12 gets twisted into a doctrine that a man may only marry his own tribe, and that is a heresy born of not knowing why the law was given.

note.label: Numbers 36: The Inheritance of the Daughters of Zelophehad

precepts.why:
Every daughter that possessed an inheritance had to marry within her father’s tribe, “that the children of Israel may enjoy every man the inheritance of his fathers”, and no inheritance would remove from one tribe to another. That restriction belonged to the time when Israel dwelt in the land; it existed because of inheritance.

Tobit told his son: “Beware of all whoredom, my son, and chiefly take a wife of the seed of thy fathers, and take not a strange woman to wife, which is not of thy father’s tribe: for we are the children of the prophets, Noe, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: remember, my son, that our fathers from the beginning, even that they all married wives of their own kindred, and were blessed in their children, and their seed shall inherit the land.”

The seed-of-thy-fathers command still stands: take a wife of the seed of thy fathers and not a strange woman. The tribe clause belonged to the inheritance law of Numbers 36. Today Israel has no inheritance in the lands of captivity, so the rule that still applies is marrying within the nation of Israel, not tribe-only marriage. No one today knows his exact tribe with certainty; a Judahite could have been dropped off anywhere in the captivity. Without the history of Numbers 36, Tobit 4:12 gets twisted into a doctrine that a man may only marry his own tribe, and that is a heresy born of not knowing why the law was given.

note.label: Deuteronomy 7: A Holy People, Chosen Above All People

precepts.why:
“Beware of all whoredom, my son, and chiefly take a wife of the seed of thy fathers, and take not a strange woman to wife, which is not of thy father’s tribe: for we are the children of the prophets, Noe, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob”. The Most High forbids marrying outside the nation.

The seed of the fathers today is found among the so-called blacks, Hispanics and Native Indians, who make up the twelve tribes of Israel. A spouse may come from any of the twelve tribes, but from within the tribes only. Our fathers from the beginning “all married wives of their own kindred, and were blessed in their children, and their seed shall inherit the land.”

“Now therefore, my son, love thy brethren, and despise not in thy heart thy brethren, the sons and daughters of thy people, in not taking a wife of them”. Going outside your nation for a husband or wife is despising your brethren in your heart. Whom you marry is the greatest commitment you make in this life; if you truly loved your people, you would choose one of your own people, “for in pride is destruction and much trouble, and in lewdness is decay and great want: for lewdness is the mother of famine.”

precepts.text: Be mindful of the Lord all your days and let not your will be set to sin or transgress His commandments; if you are not doing God's will you are doing your own will, as the nations do.
precepts.point: Let this be the reward of my adversaries from the Lord, and of them that speak evil against my soul. The adversaries are the nations, and the Lord fights for us against our enemies to save us.
precepts.why:
“My son, be mindful of the Lord our God all thy days, and let not thy will be set to sin, or to transgress his commandments: do uprightly all thy life long, and follow not the ways of unrighteousness.”

There are only two wills. If you are not doing God's will, keeping his commandments, you are doing your own will, as the nations do. That is the one in the psalm who “clothed himself with cursing like as with his garment”: his will is set to sin, and so the cursing comes into his bowels like water.
